name: Fasting insulin
summary: The level of the hormone insulin after an overnight fast. Combined with fasting glucose it gives a rough measure of insulin resistance.
why_it_matters: In insulin resistance, the pancreas makes more insulin to keep glucose normal, so fasting insulin often rises years before glucose does. That makes it an early clue to metabolic risk. But insulin assays are not standardized, values vary a lot between labs and from day to day, and there are no agreed diagnostic cutoffs, so it is best read as a trend or in context.

ref_range.source: Roche Elecsys insulin assay reference interval (fasting)
ref_range.note: Reference intervals vary considerably between assays and labs; many labs quote upper limits from about 18 to 25 uIU/mL.

deep:
## What it is

Insulin is made by pancreatic beta cells and released into the portal vein, so the liver removes about half of it before it reaches the arm. Fasting insulin reflects the amount the pancreas needs to secrete to hold overnight glucose output in check. When liver, muscle and fat become insulin-resistant, fasting insulin rises to compensate; when beta cells start to fail, insulin can fall back while glucose rises.

## Why it matters

Higher fasting insulin predicts later type 2 diabetes, and is associated with obesity, fatty liver, high triglycerides, low HDL-C, hypertension and polycystic ovary syndrome. It adds information when glucose and HbA1c are still normal. Its association with cardiovascular disease is less consistent once other risk factors are accounted for. There are no guideline-endorsed diagnostic thresholds; the ADA does not use insulin for diagnosing diabetes.

**HOMA-IR** combines the two fasting values: glucose (mg/dL) x insulin (uIU/mL) / 405 (or glucose in mmol/L x insulin / 22.5). A value of 1.0 corresponds roughly to the young, healthy reference population used to develop the model. Cutoffs quoted for "insulin resistance" range from about 1.7 to 3 depending on population and assay, so treat any single cutoff with caution.

## How to read it

Units: uIU/mL (equivalently mU/L) in the US; pmol/L elsewhere (1 uIU/mL is about 6 pmol/L; some labs use 6.945).

- Must be fasting: insulin rises several-fold within minutes of eating.
- The Roche Elecsys reference interval is 2.6-24.9 uIU/mL; other platforms differ. Insulin immunoassays are not standardized, and different methods can disagree by 20-40% or more on the same sample, so NHANES percentiles and your lab's number may not be directly comparable, and NHANES itself has changed insulin assays across cycles.
- US adults have higher fasting insulin than many leaner populations; the population median is not a healthy target, but no evidence-based optimal band exists either.

## Causes of high

Insulin resistance from obesity (especially visceral fat), inactivity, fatty liver, metabolic syndrome and early type 2 diabetes; polycystic ovary syndrome; pregnancy (especially later stages); Cushing's syndrome, acromegaly; glucocorticoids, some antipsychotics; sulfonylureas; injected insulin (depending on whether the assay detects the analogue); insulin autoimmune syndrome or anti-insulin antibodies; insulinoma (rare, with inappropriately high insulin during low glucose).

## Causes of low

Type 1 diabetes and late type 2 diabetes with beta-cell failure; pancreatitis, pancreatectomy, cystic fibrosis; prolonged fasting, very-low-carbohydrate diets and high insulin sensitivity (e.g. endurance athletes); hypopituitarism; some drugs (diazoxide, somatostatin analogues).

## What moves it

Very variable: day-to-day biological variation is around 20-30%. Recent food (even a small amount), acute stress, illness, poor sleep and glucocorticoids raise it; a recent bout of exercise and weight loss lower it. Assay matters a lot: methods differ in cross-reactivity with proinsulin and insulin analogues. **Biotin** supplements can falsely lower results on streptavidin-biotin sandwich immunoassays (including some widely used insulin assays); stopping high-dose biotin for at least 2-3 days before the draw is commonly advised. **Hemolysis** releases an insulin-degrading enzyme from red cells and can falsely lower insulin, so a haemolysed sample should be repeated.

## What to test alongside

Fasting glucose drawn at the same time (needed for HOMA-IR), HbA1c, triglycerides and HDL-C, ALT, waist circumference, and C-peptide if exogenous insulin, insulinoma or beta-cell function is the question (C-peptide is unaffected by injected insulin). An oral glucose tolerance test with insulin gives more information than a single fasting value.
